extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in U.S. politics and political commentary
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion column arguing that Senator Al Franken should not resign amid sexual-misconduct allegations, laying out standards, precedents, and political-context reasons why removal is unwarranted at this stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process via Senate Ethics Committee
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ethics Committee probe should proceed to assess the evidence with his full cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franken has returned to work while the Senate Ethics Committee pursues its investigation of his case; he should not be forced out before that process has run its course. "They should also examine..." and "the Ethics Committee probe of Franken will proceed, as it should, to assess the evidence with his full cooperation."

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity-of-offense threshold for removal
rubrics_metrics.description: The bar to removal from the Senate should be high and proportionate to the seriousness of proven misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Franken’s alleged conduct (described as "very minor by comparison") with much more serious past cases; removal should be reserved for offenses as serious as those that led to resignation or expulsion in prior precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity in treatment across parties
rubrics_metrics.description: A Democrat should be entitled to at least the same degree of due process and standards as Republicans who faced ethics probes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites David Vitter and Bob Packwood as examples and argues Franken should receive the same procedural protections and evidentiary standards applied previously to Republicans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and timing of alleged conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When the conduct occurred and whether it led to criminal charges or involved misuse of Senate resources/staff matters for assessing culpability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vitter’s conduct occurred before he ran for the Senate and didn’t result in criminal charges or involve Senate resources, which influenced the committee’s decision; such contextual factors should inform any decision about resignation or discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral mandate and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Franken was duly elected to a second term by a wide margin, removal should not be undertaken lightly and should respect the voters’ choice unless there is a compelling reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that "He was duly elected to a second term, by a wide margin, so the bar to his removal should be high"—implying electoral mandate is a substantive criterion against premature resignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public apology and contrition
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate apology and admission that conduct fell short of professed standards are relevant to evaluating whether resignation is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franken apologized immediately and admitted some conduct "had fallen short of the respect for women he has always professed," and vowed to win back trust—factors the author treats as mitigating when deciding whether he should resign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate potential orchestrated/partisan campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether allegations may be part of a coordinated campaign by political opponents (e.g., dirty tricks, bots, alt-right operatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece urges scrutiny of "intriguing clues to a right-wing campaign aimed at unseating Franken, which features Roger Stone, Russian bots and various unsavory figures on the so-called alt-right," suggesting potential political manipulation should influence how allegations are weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative culpability of other accused politicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how other politicians accused of far worse conduct (e.g., Trump, Roy Moore) are treated when judging calls for resignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author invokes Trump and Roy Moore—arguing that calls for Franken’s resignation are inconsistent if similarly or more culpable figures remain in office or unaccountable; this points to hypocrisy and consistency as evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability and willingness to continue serving
rubrics_metrics.description: If the accused no longer feels able to serve constituents or serve the country effectively, resignation may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes "he need not depart the Senate unless he no longer feels he can serve his country and his constituents," making personal capacity to serve a practical criterion for stepping down.
